doc.title: Eric Alexander interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, March 31, 2010

title: Collaborating in the studio: Joe Farnsworth's beat on 'It Might As Well Be Spring'
summary: He welcomes sidemen's input, and Farnsworth's rumba beat rescued the standard on the latest recording.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Making records: studios, takes and the technology

blocks.x: And where or when does the decision come, like you decided to have the saxophone and the bass in unison.

We may have just decided that in the studio. You know a lot of times you show up at a recording session with a very skeletal arrangement or idea of what you’re going to do, or it’s a sketch of a tune and you just kind of throw ideas around the room and everyone just pipes up with their suggestion or their criticism and after a few minutes something clicks and everyone says okay that’ll work. But people kind of have to leave their egos at the door to do that. You know you can’t come in with this idea this is how I wrote my tune and this is how it’s going to be and we’re not going to change it. Because if you do that you miss out on a lot of creativity and it’s more than a democratic process I don’t even know what you’d call it, board room last minute deals. I don’t know what it is. But you’re not utilizing your musicians to the degree that you could utilize them if you’re just going to be a dictator and say this is the way it is. If you trust and really admire the musicians you’re working with, you should welcome their input. I mean sometimes you don’t like it and sometimes they say things that you say no I don’t agree just shut up, that’s it. But sometimes, you have to listen to what they say and they may turn you on to an idea that you hadn’t thought of. It happens all the time. You know like the last recording we made we were trying to play “It Might As Well Be Spring” and I don’t even remember what groove we had on it in the rehearsal, but in the studio all of a sudden Joe Farnsworth, the drummer, said, “You know what about this beat?” and he started playing kind of a rumba or a Latin flavor beat on it. What happens if we play the tune this way? And it was like a boom. All of a sudden the tune made sense. We were kind of dreading doing it. It was just one of those standards that people will think is kind of hip if we do it but we don’t really enjoy playing it. We saved it ‘till the end of the date. And he came up with this
idea and it made it so easy to play. And it felt like our arrangement, our individual twist on it. So you have to listen to the musicians.
